title: Permutation invariant neural network prediction of vacancy formation under deformation and varying chemical environment in FCC high entropy alloys
abstract: Vacancy formation energies govern diffusion, irradiation damage, phase stability, and dynamic failure in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), yet their strong dependence on local chemical environments and mechanical deformation makes atomistic calculations prohibitively expensive for large-scale studies. Here, we develop an atomistically informed permutation invariant machine learning framework for predicting strain dependent vacancy formation energies in FCC HEAs from local atomic environments. The model employs a vacancy-centered representation constructed from objective geometric descriptors together with invariants of the local deformation gradient, enabling the coupled effects of chemical disorder and finite deformation to be learned within a unified framework. Atomistic simulations reveal that volumetric deformation is the dominant factor controlling the average variation in vacancy formation energy, whereas shear deformation has a comparatively minor influence. At the same time, substantial site to site variability persists under identical macroscopic loading, demonstrating that local chemical environments govern the statistical distribution of vacancy energetics beyond species-averaged trends. The proposed framework accurately predicts vacancy formation energies across diverse deformation states while providing orders-of-magnitude faster evaluation than direct atomistic simulations. These results establish an efficient route for incorporating stress-dependent defect energetics into multiscale models of diffusion, irradiation damage, and dynamic failure in chemically complex alloys.
summary: This work introduces an advanced machine learning framework to overcome the computational bottleneck of calculating vacancy formation energies in complex High-Entropy Alloys. By incorporating both local chemical disorder and mechanical strain into a unified, permutation invariant model, it achieves predictions orders of magnitude faster than atomistic simulations while accurately capturing site-specific defect behavior.
main_problem: Vacancy formation energies in High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) are crucial for understanding material failure, but their dependence on local chemical environments and mechanical deformation makes atomistic calculation prohibitively expensive.
main_result: The proposed ML framework accurately predicts strain-dependent vacancy formation energies orders of magnitude faster than direct simulations, confirming that local chemistry dictates defect energetics beyond simple averaging.
method: A permutation invariant machine learning framework (Deep Sets architecture) is developed to map local atomic environments and deformation gradients to vacancy formation energy.
model_or_system: The study focuses on Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs), modeling the interaction between vacancies, local chemical disorder, and applied mechanical strain/stress.
key_observables: Vacancy formation energies ($	ext{E}_{	ext{form}}$), site-to-site variability of $	ext{E}_{	ext{form}}$, and dependence on volumetric vs. shear deformation.
important_parameters: Local chemical environment, applied strain (tensile/compressive), and the specific composition of the HEA.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes that local geometric descriptors and invariants of the deformation gradient are sufficient to capture the complex coupling between chemistry and mechanics.

paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical problem (costly atomistic calculation of defect energies in HEAs) and then introduces the ML framework, detailing the use of objective geometric descriptors and deformation invariants to learn the coupled effects. Results confirm the model's accuracy and efficiency compared to direct simulations.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter defects rather than quantum information, the core methodology—using permutation invariant neural networks (Deep Sets) to encode complex local structural/chemical environments—is highly relevant for developing ML potentials or predictive models in quantum materials simulation.

Uniaxial loading produces substantial, species dependent changes in chemical potentials, reflecting the different responses of the constituent elements to volumetric deformation. In contrast, simple shear has a negligible effect on the chemical potentials, consistent with its nearly volume-preserving character.
